title: Republicans Are Losing the Populist Moment
author: Alicia Nieves
content:
![Republicans Are Losing the Populist
Moment](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/Screenshot-2026-11-08-at-10.03.46
---PM-1.png)

Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 with a second chance to
remake American politics. His victory was more than a repudiation of the Biden
administration's four years of economic and political dysfunction. It was a
powerful vindication of a man and a populist message that much of the
political establishment, including members of his own party, had spent nearly
a decade trying to defeat.

For the second time, Trump achieved electoral victory by assembling an
unlikely and diverse coalition of voters around a nationalist, anti-
establishment agenda that challenged the prevailing political consensus on
immigration, foreign policy, trade, and the progressive ideological capture of
the administrative state and major institutions of American society. And this
time, unlike in 2017, he entered Washington with an administration staffed by
people who shared his vision and with Republican majorities in both chambers
of Congress. The opportunity was enormous. After nearly a decade of political
combat, the populist electoral message finally had the opportunity to become a
lasting governing framework.

In just twenty-two months, that opportunity evaporated.

The Republican Party's sweeping defeat in the 2026 elections was not simply
another instance of voters using the midterms, as they so often do, to punish
the president's party for missteps during his first two years in office. Nor
is it adequate to explain the results solely through voter frustration over
higher prices, the Iran war, or corruption. Those issues undoubtedly fractured
Trump's electoral coalition and damaged both his personal approval rating and
the GOP's broader standing with voters. But underlying these political
liabilities was a more fundamental failure. Trump and the Republican
establishment never forged the workable political relationship needed to
transform the raucous populist insurgency that swept them into power into a
coherent, pragmatic governing agenda.
